Chinese Semiconductor Equipment Makers Accelerate Localization Beyond Front-End Processes into Advanced Packaging

Major Chinese semiconductor equipment manufacturers are accelerating efforts to localize back-end processing equipment by leveraging technologies they have already developed for front-end wafer fabrication.

According to industry sources on Sept. 5, Chinese semiconductor equipment companies including NAURA Technology, Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment Inc. China (AMEC), and Hwatsing Technology are extending their existing expertise in etching, deposition, and chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) beyond front-end processes into equipment specifically designed for back-end applications such as hybrid bonding, dicing, and wafer thinning.

The move is seen as part of China’s broader push to expand semiconductor equipment self-sufficiency into advanced packaging amid U.S. export restrictions on chipmaking equipment. In particular, as the expansion of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and three-dimensional chip stacking increasingly blurs the boundary between front-end and back-end processes, there is greater scope for existing front-end technologies to be adapted for packaging applications.

NAURA, China’s largest semiconductor equipment manufacturer, recently said in its first-half earnings report that it had launched two types of 12-inch hybrid bonding systems: wafer-to-wafer (WTW) and die-to-wafer (DTW). The DTW system has already entered the customer application stage.

Hybrid bonding is a precision bonding technology used to densely stack multiple chips, such as in HBM and chiplet architectures.

This year, NAURA also introduced equipment for through-silicon via (TSV) electroplating and panel-level packaging (PLP) processes. Its advanced-packaging portfolio now spans equipment that fills microscopic TSV holes with copper to enable vertical chip interconnection, as well as systems used for redistribution-layer formation and surface treatment on large panels.

AMEC, China’s leading etching equipment supplier, is also expanding beyond its existing TSV etching business into dicing and deposition. Its plasma dicing equipment, which separates wafers into individual dies, has progressed to the customer qualification stage at major Chinese customers this year.

In the first half of the year, AMEC also began developing deposition equipment for under-bump metallization (UBM), which forms the metal layer beneath chip interconnect bumps.

AMEC has set a target of addressing more than 70% of the equipment categories required for advanced packaging over the next five years through a combination of in-house R&D and mergers and acquisitions. The company plans to broaden its packaging equipment portfolio from its traditional focus on TSV etching into dicing and deposition.

Hwatsing Technology, whose core business is CMP equipment, is similarly expanding the application of its existing technologies into advanced packaging. After supplying certain advanced CMP tools to HBM production lines at major Chinese memory manufacturers, the company has added dedicated packaging equipment for wafer thinning and edge processing. In the first half of this year, it shipped its first new 12-inch wafer thinning system designed for advanced memory applications.

Oh Jong-hyuk, a researcher at the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP), said, “China faces constraints in advancing leading-edge semiconductor processes due to U.S. equipment export controls, and is therefore pursuing advanced packaging as a way to compensate for the performance limitations of individual chips. As architectures that connect multiple chips to increase aggregate computing power become more important, the scope of equipment localization is also expanding into back-end processes.”

However, many of the newly announced systems from Chinese vendors are still undergoing customer qualification or remain in the early stages of commercialization. Their ability to demonstrate competitive yields, equipment uptime, stability, and productivity in actual high-volume manufacturing lines will be a key factor determining whether they can achieve broader market adoption.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Sep 5, 2026

The modules reportedly reduce read latency to one-tenth or less of that of existing products, bringing performance closer to DRAM. Kioxia said replacing some DRAM with CXL modules could double capacity and improve performance by 30%.

items.content:
MICRON TO DOUBLE HBM PRODUCTION CAPACITY, NARROWING GAP WITH SAMSUNG AND SK HYNIX

U.S. memory maker Micron plans to double its high-bandwidth memory (HBM) production capacity from last year. Through aggressive capital spending by year-end, the company aims to strengthen its supply capabilities for 12-high HBM4, the latest generation of HBM. The move is intended to increase its market share by expanding its HBM capacity, which currently trails that of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.

According to industry sources on September 3, Micron plans to add up to 60,000 wafers per month of HBM production capacity by the end of this year. The net addition would exceed the company’s HBM production level of roughly 40,000–50,000 wafers per month last year.

“Micron is making substantial investments in equipment to rapidly ramp up its HBM4 production capacity,” said an industry source familiar with the matter. “By the end of this year, it will have secured HBM production capacity of approximately 100,000 wafers per month.”

To achieve this expansion, Micron is increasing purchase orders (POs) with multiple HBM equipment suppliers. Equipment deliveries are understood to be ongoing at its HBM manufacturing sites in Taiwan and Singapore.

The share of 12-high HBM4 in Micron’s production mix is expected to rise significantly. Currently, 12-high HBM3E accounts for most of its HBM output. As recently as early this year, 12-high HBM4 represented only 20–30% of the total, but that share is reportedly set to reach as much as 50% by year-end.

Twelve-high HBM4 will be used in Vera Rubin, the latest AI accelerator from NVIDIA, the world’s largest AI chip company. Micron began mass production of its 12-high HBM4 products in the second quarter of this year.

During Micron’s fiscal third-quarter 2026 earnings announcement in June, CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said, “We are ramping up 12-high HBM4 production at roughly twice the pace of 12-high HBM3E,” adding that “cumulative revenue from HBM4 shipments has exceeded $1 billion.”

Although Micron is one of the world’s three major HBM manufacturers, its production capacity falls short of Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. Industry estimates put each Korean company’s HBM capacity at approximately 150,000–200,000 wafers per month—three to four times Micron’s level. Unless Micron catches up with their production capacity, it will struggle to escape its position as a perennial third-place player.

If Micron meets its capacity target this year, it could roughly halve its production gap with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.

Micron’s HBM capacity expansion also underscores the strength of demand for AI memory. Supply continues to fall short of demand as AI chipmakers, led by NVIDIA, seek large volumes of HBM. In this environment, maximizing HBM earnings requires the ability to supply more products—in other words, sufficient production capacity.

Micron is investing in HBM manufacturing facilities around the world. In addition to its investments in the United States, the company carries out HBM packaging at its Tongluo fab in Taiwan and Woodlands fab in Singapore, and is preparing equipment investments in Hiroshima, Japan.

According to Counterpoint Research, SK hynix led the global HBM market with a 50% share in the second quarter of this year, followed by Samsung Electronics at 32% and Micron at 18%.

items.content:
I was reading through ITEQ’s Q&A and found a few interesting comments:

1. “It is clear that glass-fiber fabric prices are rising, and we still expect a double-digit increase in the second half.”

2. It is uncertain how long the rise in glass-fiber prices will continue. From ITEQ’s perspective, however, we also need to consider that the large Chinese glass-fiber manufacturers we work with are pursuing very aggressive capacity-expansion plans.

3. If ITEQ can increase its use of glass-fiber fabric supplied by these Chinese manufacturers, it may not feel the Nittobo supply shortage as acutely as it does today.

4. Analyst: “Still, aren’t Nittobo’s supply shortages and price increases positive for CCL makers such as ITEQ?” ITEQ: “From a pricing perspective, yes. Nittobo has the broadest and most mature portfolio of high-end glass-fiber fabrics, giving it sufficient bargaining power to raise prices. Chinese fabric suppliers, however, are also expanding capacity aggressively and improving their technology. Whether they can actually reach the Low Dk 1 and 2 levels remains to be proven. Even so, the fabric shortage across the CCL industry is currently so severe that ITEQ plans to qualify and utilize as many Chinese suppliers as possible.”
— Jukan (@jukan05) Sep 3, 2026
